title: Mind training
hook: short Tibetan slogans, carried in the pocket, meant to go off at the worst moment

segments.voice: Yesterday, the alms round at first light. Your word was dana, giving. Did you hand someone food, and notice the before, the during and the after? Today we leave the Theravada world and cross the mountains into Tibetan Buddhism. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-four.

A coworker drops the ball, again, and the reply taking shape on the screen gets a little sharper with every line. By the third paragraph it's a closing argument. It's a familiar shape of moment: the point when the mind has already decided whose fault it is and is busy building the case. Tibetan Buddhism has a set of tools made for exactly that moment. They're not long meditations. They're slogans, short enough to remember in the middle of a bad afternoon, built to go off right when the case-building starts. One of them is your line today, and it sounds, at first, like terrible advice. Today's word is the whole toolkit.
screen: `THE EMAIL GETS SHARPER.` → `THE MIND BUILDS A CASE.` → `A SLOGAN FOR THAT MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Lojong is Tibetan for mind training. Tibetan tradition traces these teachings to the Indian teacher Atisha, and says a Tibetan teacher, Geshe Chekawa, set them down as a list of short slogans. Four turns. First, the form. A slogan isn't something to sit and study once. It's something to memorize and carry, so it surfaces on its own in traffic, in a meeting, at the sink. The training happens out there, not only on the cushion. Second, your line: drive all blames into one. It sounds like everything is your fault. That isn't what the teachers mean. The one is a habit inside us that puts our own comfort at the center of everything, what the tradition calls self-cherishing. When something goes wrong, the slogan says, look there first. Not at yourself as a bad person. At the reflex that was already writing the closing argument. Third, trouble becomes the path. Another slogan, in paraphrase, says that when hard things happen, turn them into practice. The difficult coworker isn't an interruption of the training. The difficult coworker is the training. Fourth, gratitude. One more slogan, in paraphrase: be grateful to everyone. Including, the commentaries say, the people who make life hard, because without them there'd be nothing to train with. It's a strange kind of thank-you note, and lojong teachers mean it. Put together, the slogans don't ask anyone to pretend nothing went wrong. They ask the mind to change where it points when it does.
screen: `SLOGANS TO CARRY, NOT STUDY.` · `THE ONE IS SELF-CHERISHING.` · `TROUBLE BECOMES THE PATH.` · `GRATEFUL TO EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one slogan. There are three from today: drive all blames into one; turn hard things into the path; be grateful to everyone. Sit, and settle the breath. Choose the one that bothers you a little. That's often the useful one. Now bring up a recent moment when you were building a case against someone. Hold the slogan up next to it, quietly, the way you'd hold a key up to a lock. No need to force a result. Just let them sit together. The bell holds the time.
Lojong. Mind training, in Tibetan Buddhism: short slogans, traced by tradition to Atisha, carried into daily life and used right when trouble comes. Today's word.
Your line: drive all blames into one. Today, the next time the mind starts building a case, say the line once, and look first at the reflex, not the person. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists who practice lojong often memorize the mind-training slogans, study them with a teacher's commentary, and recall them during daily life, especially in difficult moments.

what a scholar hears: a slogan tradition traced to Atisha and set down by Geshe Chekawa, where the one to blame is self-cherishing.

notes: The outline's '12th century' and the slogan count were left out under the claims rule.
'Drive all blames into one' is the index carry and a common modern English rendering; it is used as the line, not presented as a quotation from a public-domain translation.
Slogans 'transform hard circumstances into the path' and 'be grateful to everyone' are paraphrased; confirm wording and that they belong to the Seven-Point Mind Training.
Explanation of 'the one' as self-cherishing (rang gces 'dzin) follows standard commentaries; confirm.
Tibetan script བློ་སྦྱོང་ and pronunciation 'LO-jong'; confirm.
Editor pass: hook and fork no longer tell the listener they are writing the sharp email; the reply is described as a scene on the screen.
